title: Hot work on drums, tanks and cylinders
summary: Cutting, grinding, welding or heating a drum, tank or cylinder that held fuel, oil, solvent or anything unknown can blow it apart, even when it looks empty and has stood for years. Find out what it held, empty and clean it, fill it with water or purge it, keep it vented and cut cold. Never put a grinder or torch on a closed vessel.

materials.item: Plenty of clean water and a hose
materials.qty: enough to fill the vessel twice

materials.item: Proprietary degreasing detergent (industrial, not household) for boiling
Drum-opening tool, hand hacksaw or air chisel for cold cutting
Leather gloves, and chemical gloves for corrosives
ABC fire extinguisher or water ready

steps.text: Find out what the vessel held: label, stencil, hazard diamond, the person who used it. Treat anything unknown as dangerous, because drums get reused and labels lie (NZ OSH drums, HSE drum bulletin).
steps.warn: If you don't know what it held, don't put heat on it (WorkSafe Vic drums). Organochlorine pesticide drums (aldrin, DDT, lindane and the like) and carbon tetrachloride can make phosgene when heated (NZ OSH drums).

steps.text: Ask whether you need heat at all: another container, a cold cut or a cold repair often does the job (HSE INDG314, CSB hot work).

Work outdoors on bare ground, away from buildings and anything that burns, with water or an extinguisher at hand. Wear eye protection, leather gloves and overalls; chemical gloves and a face shield for corrosives (NZ OSH drums).
steps.warn: Keep everyone back and out of line with the ends: drum and tank ends are what fly (HSE INDG314, NZ OSH drums).

steps.text: Take out every cap, bung and lid, with non-sparking bronze tools if you have them, and drain or pump the contents into a container (NZ OSH drums, HSE INDG314).
steps.warn: Never drain a fuel tank over a pit or hole, where vapour gathers (NZ OSH drums).

steps.text: Clean it. Wash with water only for contents that dissolve in water; for petrol, oil, grease, solvents or anything unknown, boil it fully under water with a proprietary degreasing detergent (not household dish soap) for at least 30 minutes, or steam it, drum upside down, for 30 minutes after every part is too hot to touch (NZ OSH drums).
steps.warn: Never wash it out with a flammable cleaner and cap it: that is how an Ottawa student was killed in 2011 (CHRR Ottawa).

steps.text: Inspect inside with a light and by smell. Sludge or smell left means clean it again (NZ OSH drums, HSE INDG314).
steps.warn: A gas meter can't see residue that boils off once the steel is hot (NZ OSH drums). Never test with a flame (CSB hot work).

steps.text: Fill it with water: right to the top for electric welding, or to just below the work for a gas torch (NZ OSH drums, OSHA 1926.352).
steps.warn: Always leave a vent so steam can escape (NZ OSH drums). Never heat a sealed vessel full of water.

steps.text: Water is the method for a home job. Only if water can't be used, purge with CO2 from dry ice: at least 0.5 kg per 250 L, in tanks up to about 1,000 L, with the filling opening vented through a simple non-return valve so pressure can't build (NZ OSH drums). HSE says inert gas needs an oxygen meter to show air hasn't crept back, and should be left to specialists (HSE INDG314).
steps.warn: CO2 and nitrogen don't support life: never put your head into an inerted tank (NZ OSH drums).

steps.text: Keep at least one opening open for the whole job so air and gas can get out (OSHA 1910.252, WorkSafe Vic drums).
Cut cold where you can: a drum-opening tool, hydraulic shears, an air chisel or an air hacksaw. Take the top off first so you can see inside and the vessel has some pressure relief (HSE INDG314).
steps.warn: Cold cutting still heats the metal a little (HSE INDG314), and even a spark from a mechanical tool can light petrol vapour (NZ OSH drums): clean and fill first anyway.

steps.text: Never put a grinder, torch, plasma cutter or welder on a closed vessel, and never use a drum as a bench, stand or seat for hot work (NZ OSH drums, HSE INDG314).
steps.warn: A lacquer-thinner drum with its bungs in hit a roof 6 m up when heat went on the lid (NZ OSH drums).

steps.text: Propane and other gas cylinders: hand them to a propane supplier if one exists (CT DEEP propane). Don't take a valve out yourself, and don't cut or drill the cylinder (CT DEEP propane, gas cylinders card). If no supplier exists, leave it upright outdoors with the valve shut, away from buildings and heat. Weigh it against the tare weight stamped on its collar before calling it empty (TSBC BLEVE).
steps.warn: Every used cylinder still holds gas (CT DEEP propane). Weigh it rather than trusting a hiss: propane boils at −42 °C (TSBC BLEVE).

steps.text: Air tanks: drain the water and oil, prove there is no pressure, take out the fittings, then clean it as an oil container and fill it with water (CP condensate, NZ OSH drums).
steps.warn: Loosen nothing until the tank is proved empty: see the air compressor teardown.

steps.text: After any hot work, stay and watch for smouldering for at least 30 minutes (OSHA 1910.252).

notes:
## Why "empty" drums blow up
Hot work is anything that makes flame, sparks or heat: welding, torch cutting, grinding and sawing (HSE INDG314). A drum, tank or cylinder that seems empty usually still has residue in the bottom, the seams and the crevices, and HSE says a teaspoon of petrol in a drum can be enough for an explosion once heat turns it to vapour (HSE INDG314). A drum left empty out in the weather for years can still hold enough in its seams (NZ OSH drums). The blast can burst eardrums and damage the lungs, throw fragments, and throw you (NZ OSH drums).

It isn't only petrol. Vessels to treat as dangerous (NZ OSH drums, HSE drum bulletin, WorkSafe Vic drums):
- **Volatile liquids:** petrol, thinners, acetone, white spirit, solvents.
- **Oils and solids that give off vapour only when heated:** diesel, engine oil, grease, tar, linseed oil, tallow, soap, paint residue, and other oils and fats that give off vapour when heated (engine oil and paint residue: HSE INDG314).
- **Acids**, which react with steel to make hydrogen.
- **Fine powders** that can explode as a dust cloud: flour, sugar, milk powder, sulphur.
- **Pesticides and carbon tetrachloride**: some organochlorine insecticides and carbon tetrachloride form phosgene, a poison gas, when heated (NZ OSH drums). Don't heat these at all.
- **Even water tanks**: at a Wisconsin fibreboard mill in 2008, bacteria in a tank of recycled water and fibre waste made hydrogen, and a welding spark killed three workers (CSB hot work).

## What it held
Read the label, the stencilling and the hazard diamonds, but don't trust them: drums get reused, so the contents may not match the label (NZ OSH drums, HSE drum bulletin). A UN mark starting 1A1 is a steel drum with a fixed top and bungs; 1A2 has a removable lid (Cary drums). Neither code tells you what was inside: drums get reused, so contents may not match the label (HSE drum bulletin). If you can't find out, treat it as the worst case: WorkSafe Victoria says don't apply heat to a container whose contents you don't know (WorkSafe Vic drums).

## Clean it
1. **Isolate and empty.** Take the vessel off anything it's piped to, then drain or pump it out into a container (HSE INDG314). Take out every cap, bung and lid, with non-sparking (bronze) tools if you have them (NZ OSH drums). Never drain a fuel tank over a pit or hole, where vapour collects (NZ OSH drums).
2. **Wash with water** only for things that dissolve in water, such as acids. Water won't shift petrol, oil, grease or solvents (NZ OSH drums), and rinsing alone doesn't guarantee the residue and vapour are gone (WorkSafe Vic drums).
3. **Boil or steam** anything else, or anything you can't identify (NZ OSH drums):
   - *Boiling:* the drum fully under boiling water with a degreasing detergent, for at least half an hour, often longer. Strong caustic cleaners attack aluminium and give off hydrogen.
   - *Steaming:* low-pressure steam with an outlet so pressure can't build, the drum upside down so condensate and sludge drain. At least 30 minutes after every part is too hot to touch; some items need 2 to 3 hours. Keep going while the condensate still shows oil.
4. **Don't** blow it out with compressed air: it can move vapour but leaves solids that give off more (NZ OSH drums). **Don't** clean it with a flammable cleaner and then close it up: an Ottawa high-school drum washed out with a flammable cleaner and stored with its caps on exploded when a student cut it with a grinder in 2011, killing him (CHRR Ottawa).
5. **Inspect.** Look inside with a light, and smell. Any light you put inside must be made for flammable atmospheres. If you can still smell it or see sludge, clean it again (NZ OSH drums, HSE INDG314).

## Gas meters and what they miss
A combustible gas (LEL) meter reads the vapour that's there now, at air temperature. It can't see sludge or oil that will boil off once the steel is hot, so a zero reading doesn't make a vessel safe (NZ OSH drums, HSE INDG314). Where you have one, test before and during the work; NFPA 326 says stop all work if the reading reaches 10% of the lower explosive limit (CSB hot work). Never test with a flame. At an oilfield in Raleigh, Mississippi, in 2006, workers checked a tank for vapour with a lit torch instead of a meter; welding sparks then lit vapour from the tanks and three died (CSB hot work). CSB asks for a properly calibrated combustible gas detector (CSB hot work).

## Fill it or purge it
Cleaning comes first; filling is the extra safeguard, and the main one when the residue won't all come out (NZ OSH drums, HSE INDG314).
- **Water** is the easiest for drums and vehicle fuel tanks. Fill it completely for electric welding, or to just below the spot you are working on for a gas torch, and give the steam a vent (NZ OSH drums).
- **Carbon dioxide from dry ice:** at least 0.5 kg per 250 L of tank, in tanks up to about 1,000 L; CO2 sinks, so it must not leak out of a low opening, and the filling opening needs a simple non-return valve so pressure can't build (NZ OSH drums). Handle dry ice with gloves or tongs (NZ OSH drums). HSE says inert gases need an oxygen meter to show air hasn't crept back in, and should be left to specialists (HSE INDG314): use water where you can.
- **Nitrogen** needs an oxygen meter and is specialist work (HSE INDG314, NZ OSH drums).
- CO2 and nitrogen don't support life: never put your head or body into an inerted tank, and never climb into any tank to clean or cut it (NZ OSH drums). See [confined spaces](#browse/hazards/confined_space).

## Vent it and cut cold
Every hollow space must have an opening so air and gas can escape before any heat goes on; US rules recommend an inert-gas purge as well (OSHA 1910.252). Leave the bungs out (WorkSafe Vic drums). Cold cutting is the safer choice: hydraulic shears, an air chisel or air hacksaw, or a drum-opening tool like big tin snips (HSE INDG314, NZ OSH drums). Take the top off first if you can: you can then see inside, and it gives some pressure relief (HSE INDG314). Even a spark from a mechanical tool can light petrol vapour (NZ OSH drums), so clean and fill the vessel first even for a cold cut.

Never put a grinder, torch, plasma cutter or welder on a closed vessel. A drum of lacquer thinner with both bungs in hit a roof 6 m up when heat went on its lid (NZ OSH drums). A tank end flew 42 m, over a stand of 12 m trees, when a cut was started (NZ OSH drums). Never use a drum as a bench, a stand or something to sit on while doing hot work: people have been burned that way (HSE INDG314, NZ OSH drums).

## Propane and other gas cylinders
Every used propane tank still holds some gas, and Connecticut's environment department says not to try to take the valve out yourself: doing it safely needs special equipment and training (CT DEEP propane). Hand an old cylinder to a propane supplier if one still operates. The card for [gas cylinders](#browse/hazards/compressed_gas) says never cut or drill one, even empty.

Propane boils at −42 °C (TSBC BLEVE), so a cylinder in deep cold can still hold liquid while hardly pushing any gas out. Judge "empty" with the cylinder warm, by weighing it against the empty weight (TW) stamped on the collar. Heat raises the pressure inside; if the cylinder fails, the liquid flash-boils into a cloud that can become a fireball and blast (TSBC BLEVE).

This card gives no home method for opening a propane cylinder. Connecticut's environment department says removing the valve takes special equipment and training (CT DEEP propane), and the water-fill rule above can't be followed while the valve is fitted. If no supplier exists, leave the cylinder alone, upright outdoors with the valve shut, away from buildings and heat, and use a clean drum for whatever you were going to build.

## Air tanks and vehicle tanks
- **Compressor tanks:** drain them and prove there's no pressure before you loosen anything ([air compressor teardown](#guides/teardown_air_compressor)). The water inside carries oil and rust (CP condensate), and oil residue vaporises when heated (NZ OSH drums), so clean it as an oil container (boil or steam) and fill it with water before cutting.
- **Vehicle fuel tanks:** drain them fully, take them off the vehicle, keep sparks and flames well away, and fill with water (NZ OSH drums). A two-compartment tank needs both compartments made safe (NZ OSH drums).

## When no help is coming
- **The safest drum is a different drum.** If you can't find out what it held or can't boil or steam it, use a drum you know held only water, or open it cold, by hand, full of water.
- **Work outdoors**, away from buildings, fuel and dry grass, with an extinguisher or water at hand (NZ OSH drums). Keep everyone else well back and out of line with the ends: ends are what fly. Stay with the job at least half an hour after hot work stops, watching for smouldering (OSHA 1910.252); longer is better. Eye, fume and grinder rules: [Welding and cutting](#guides/reference_welding_cutting).
- **If it hisses, bulges, smokes from inside or flames at a bung while you work:** stop, step back out of line with the ends, and let it burn out. Don't try to cap it. A burning opening can spray fuel onto clothing (NZ OSH drums).
- **A gas cylinder in a fire** can burst into a fireball (TSBC BLEVE). Get everyone well away, behind something solid, and let it burn; the [sealed containers card](#browse/hazards/sealed_heating) gives evacuation distances.
- **A propane cylinder isn't worth the risk for a stove body or forge.** A clean steel drum does the job: [Barrel stove](#guides/build_barrel_stove).
- **Burns:** cool under running water, ideally for 20 minutes, and cover loosely ([hot surfaces](#browse/hazards/burn), [burns over days](#ref/reference_first_aid/burns_over_days)).
- **A blast** can burst eardrums, hurt the lungs and drive in fragments, and it can throw a person against something hard (NZ OSH drums). Check for all of these: [first aid when no help is coming](#ref/reference_first_aid/when_no_help_is_coming).
- **Residues:** don't tip them into drains, ditches or streams (HSE INDG314); keep them well away from any well or water you drink.
